title: Subject-Verb Concord: Finding the Real Subject

blocks.text: "The long list of approved textbooks are on the notice board." It sounds acceptable because *textbooks* is the last thing your ear heard. But only one thing is on the board — the list. Almost every concord question in WAEC and JAMB is built on exactly this trick: a plural noun placed between the subject and the verb.

blocks.title: Concord
blocks.text: Agreement between a subject and its verb in number and person. A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. Concord is decided by the grammatical subject alone, never by the nearest noun.

blocks.markdown:
### The master technique: cover the middle

Most concord errors disappear if you delete everything between the subject and the verb, especially phrases beginning with *of*, *with*, *together with*, *as well as*, *along with*, *including* and *in addition to*.

- The long list ~~of approved textbooks~~ **is** on the notice board.
- The Governor, ~~along with his commissioners~~, **was** at the ceremony.
- Each ~~of the candidates~~ **has** been given a booklet.

Only *and* genuinely creates a plural subject. The other joining expressions leave the original subject untouched.

rows: The box of files is missing.
*Either ... or*, *neither ... nor* take the nearer subject
Neither the principal nor the teachers were present.
Each of the girls has a lamp.
Nouns in -s that name one field are singular
Amounts, distances and periods are singular
Twenty years is a long time.
*The number of* is singular; *a number of* is plural
The number of pupils is rising. A number of pupils are absent.
The jury are divided in their opinions.

blocks.title: Solving a concord question in five seconds
blocks.prompt: Complete the sentence: "One of the boys who ______ selected for the quiz is my cousin."

steps.text: Notice that the sentence has two verbs to account for: the blank, and *is* near the end.
Find the subject of *is*. It is *One*, which is singular — and the sentence already supplies the correct singular verb.
Now find the subject of the blank. The blank belongs to the relative clause opened by *who*.
Ask what *who* refers back to. It was the boys who were selected, not the one cousin, so the antecedent is the plural *boys*.
A relative pronoun takes its number from its antecedent, so the verb in the relative clause must be plural: *were*.
Read the finished sentence: 'One of the boys who were selected for the quiz is my cousin.' A plural and a singular verb sit in one sentence, and both are correct.

blocks.answer: were — the relative pronoun *who* refers to the plural *boys*, while *is* agrees separately with the singular *One*

blocks.markdown:
### Collective nouns cut both ways

A collective noun such as *jury*, *team*, *committee*, *government*, *family* or *class* takes:

- a **singular** verb when the group acts as one body — *The committee **has** published its report.*
- a **plural** verb when the members act individually — *The jury **are** divided in **their** opinions.*

The pronoun you use later in the sentence must match the choice you made. *Its* goes with the singular; *their* goes with the plural. Mixing them is a clear error.

items: *There is* / *There are* agrees with the noun that follows: *There **are** two candidates left.*
A title or a single work is singular even if plural in form: *Things Fall Apart **is** a great novel.*
Two nouns naming one thing take a singular verb: *Bread and butter **is** all he wants for breakfast.*
*Many a* is singular: *Many a student **has** failed for this reason.*
*None of* is usually singular in formal writing: *None of the money **was** recovered.*

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: When you meet a concord question, put your pen over every word between the subject and the blank before you choose. If the sentence contains *either ... or* or *neither ... nor*, look only at the subject nearer to the verb. Those two habits answer the majority of concord items correctly.

points: Concord depends on the grammatical subject, not on the nearest noun.
Cover phrases beginning with *of*, *with* or *as well as* to reveal the true subject.
Only *and* creates a plural subject; *along with* and *as well as* do not.
*Either ... or* and *neither ... nor* agree with the nearer subject.
Each, every, either, neither and the -body pronouns are singular.
Amounts, distances, periods and field names ending in -s take singular verbs.
A relative pronoun takes its number from its antecedent.
